etymologies.etymologyHTML: From French académie, from Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía), a grove of trees and gymnasium outside of Athens where Plato taught; from the name of the supposed former owner of that estate, the Attic hero Akademos. Doublet of academia and Akademeia; compare academe.

definitions.definition: (classical studies, usually capitalized) The garden where Plato taught. [First attested around 1350 to 1470.][1]
(classical studies, usually capitalized) Plato's philosophical system based on skepticism; Plato's followers. [First attested in the mid 16th century.][1]
An institution for the study of higher learning; a college or a university; typically a private school. [First attested in the mid 16th century.][1]

quote.citation: 1760–5, Tobias Smollett, The history of England from the revolution in 1688, to the death of George II, published 1805, page 449:
quote.text: The artists of London had long maintained a private academy for improvement in the art of drawing from living figures

quote.citation: 1776, David Hume, The life of David Hume‎[1]:
quote.text: In this year 1633, I became acquainted with Nicholas Fiske, licentiate in physic, who was born in Suffolk, near Framingham* Castle, of very good parentage, who educated him at country schools, until he was fit for the university; but he went not to the academy, studying at home both astrology and physic, which he afterwards practised in Colchester; and there was well acquainted with Dr Gilbert, who wrote "De Magnete".

definitions.definition: A school or place of training in which some special art is taught. [First attested in the late 16th century.][1]

quote.citation: 1956, Delano Ames, chapter 9, in Crime out of Mind‎[2]:
quote.text: Rudolf was the bold, bad Baron of traditional melodrama. Irene was young, as pretty as a picture, fresh from a music academy in England. He was the scion of an ancient noble family; she an orphan without money or friends.

definitions.definition: A society of learned people united for the advancement of the arts and sciences, and literature, or some particular art or science. [First attested in the early 17th century.][1]
(obsolete) The knowledge disseminated in an Academy. [Attested from the early 17th century until the mid 18th century.][1]
(with the, without reference to any specific academy) Academia.

quote.citation: 2016, Neoliberal Tools (and Archives): A Political History of Digital Humanities‎[3]:
quote.text: In the academy and outside of it, the privileging of technical expertise above other forms of knowledge is a political gesture, and one that has proved highly effective in neutralizing critique of established power relations.

definitions.definition: A body of established opinion in a particular field, regarded as authoritative.
(UK, education) A school directly funded by central government, independent of local control.
